title: The Belief Required for Super Bowl Stardom
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using the story of NFL running back Saquon Barkley, the post argues that a leader's belief in someone can change the course of a life. A Rutgers coach saw Division 1 potential in a junior-varsity sophomore, advocated for a scholarship, and years later reminded Barkley of it after a game. Barkley still credits that moment for his career. The author generalizes the anecdote into a leadership principle: great leaders and mentors see what people might become before those people can see it themselves. The post closes by asking readers to remember who believed in them and to consider who will one day say the same of them.
points: Great leaders respond to a person's future potential, not merely their current performance.
Having a champion creates a tailwind of confidence that lets people stretch beyond what they imagined possible.
The Wilson-Barkley story shows that belief extended early can be remembered and valued for decades, even when the person ultimately goes elsewhere.
The closing question turns the story inward, asking leaders whose life they will have shaped by their belief.
quotes: Norries Wilson, the running back coach at Rutgers University, saw something in Barkley’s game films that others hadn’t yet noticed. Wilson advocated for offering the young man a Division 1 scholarship — an unheard-of offer for a JV player.

Barkley, now a star NFL running back in today’s Super Bowl, still gets emotional telling this story. “That’s all you need sometimes,” said Barkley. “Someone to believe in you and take a chance on you. I’m forever grateful. I don’t think I ever get to this point if not for that moment.

Like Coach Wilson, great leaders and mentors see potential in people before they see it in themselves. They don’t just believe in what someone can do today. They believe in what that person might become tomorrow.

Having someone firmly in your corner, someone who believes in your potential and champions your success, creates a tailwind for success. It gives them the confidence to stretch and to become more than they imagined possible.
In a twist of fate, Barkley’s first collegiate start came against Rutgers, where Wilson was serving as the interim coach.
